questions.prompt: "Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things" is:
questions.explain: Waldo Tobler, 1970.

questions.prompt: If a map looks clustered, it is clustered.
questions.explain: Seeing a pattern is subjective, and classification and colors change what we see. Test it.

questions.prompt: A statistic that gives one value for the whole study area is:
questions.explain: It doesn't tell you where clusters are.

questions.prompt: Which kind of statistic can be mapped to show where clusters are?
questions.explain: Local statistics give a value for every observation.

questions.prompt: Points spread out in a regular, repeating way are:
questions.explain: Also called ordered.

questions.prompt: An Average Nearest Neighbor ratio of 0.57 means the points are:
questions.explain: Below 1: closer together than random.

questions.prompt: The ANN ratio takes the attribute values of the points into account.
questions.explain: ANN uses locations only. For values, use spatial autocorrelation.

questions.prompt: Drawing a larger study area around the same points makes their ANN ratio:
choices: Smaller, so they look more clustered
Larger, so they look more dispersed
questions.explain: The expected distance grows with the area. Always report the study area.

questions.prompt: You have hospital locations with no attributes. Which method can you use?
questions.explain: Moran's I and Gi* need values.

questions.prompt: The "auto" in spatial autocorrelation means:
choices: One variable compared with itself at nearby locations
questions.explain: Correlation between two variables is a different question.

questions.prompt: Why use rates instead of raw counts for spatial autocorrelation?
choices: Places with more people have more cases just because of their size
Moran's I only works on percentages
questions.explain: Use rates or densities, such as cases per 1,000 residents.

questions.prompt: A perfect checkerboard of two values has a Moran's I of:
questions.explain: Every neighbor is the opposite value: perfectly dispersed.

questions.prompt: A Moran's I near 0 means the values are:
questions.explain: The expected value under randomness is −1/(N − 1), close to 0.

questions.prompt: When two neighbors are both above the mean, their product in the Moran's I formula is:
questions.explain: Alike neighbors give positive products; unlike neighbors, negative.

questions.prompt: Moran's I = 0.158 with *p* = 0.028 describes a pattern that is:
questions.explain: 0.1 to 0.3 is slightly clustered, and *p* < 0.05.

questions.prompt: *I* = 0.04 with *p* < 0.001, from thousands of observations. Best description:
choices: Statistically significant but essentially random in practice
questions.explain: With many observations, tiny deviations become significant. Interpret both I and p.

questions.prompt: A Monte Carlo (permutation) test for Moran's I:
choices: Shuffles the values across locations many times and compares the observed I with the shuffled ones
Adds random noise to the coordinates
questions.explain: `moran.mc()` in spdep.

questions.prompt: A county with a large positive Gi* z-score is a:
questions.explain: High values surrounded by high values.

questions.prompt: An area of low values surrounded by low values is a:
questions.explain: It has a large negative z-score.

questions.prompt: A Gi* z-score of 2.3 is significant at the 0.05 level.
questions.explain: |z| above 1.96 is significant at 0.05.

questions.prompt: How does Gi* differ from Gi?
choices: Gi* includes the observation itself along with its neighbors
questions.explain: In spdep, `include.self()` turns Gi into Gi*.

questions.prompt: Wake County had a high birth density in the 1970s but was not a Gi* hot spot. Why?
choices: Its neighbors had much lower values, so the neighborhood as a whole wasn't unusual
questions.explain: Gi* finds clusters of high values, not single high values.

questions.prompt: Complete the code for a Monte Carlo test of Moran's I with 499 simulations.
questions.explain: `moran.test()` is the formula version.

questions.prompt: Which spdep function gives a Gi z-score for every observation?
questions.explain: Use binary weights with `include.self()` for Gi*.

questions.prompt: `moranI()` calculates Moran's I. Make `halves`, an 8 × 8 grid that is 0 in the left four columns and 1 in the right four (use `cells$col`), and store its Moran's I in `I`.
questions.solution:
cells <- expand.grid(row = 1:8, col = 1:8)
W <- (as.matrix(dist(cells)) == 1) * 1
moranI <- function(x, W) {
  z <- x - mean(x)
  (length(x) / sum(W)) * sum(W * outer(z, z)) / sum(z^2)
}

halves <- as.integer(cells$col > 4)
I <- moranI(halves, W)
questions.explain: Two solid halves give I = 0.857: strongly clustered.

questions.prompt: Store in `Do` the mean distance from each point to its nearest neighbor.
questions.starter:
x <- c(1, 2, 1, 8, 9)
y <- c(1, 1, 2, 8, 8)
d <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(x, y)))
diag(d) <- Inf
questions.solution:
x <- c(1, 2, 1, 8, 9)
y <- c(1, 1, 2, 8, 8)
d <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(x, y)))
diag(d) <- Inf
Do <- mean(apply(d, 1, min))
questions.explain: Every point's nearest neighbor is 1 unit away, so the mean is 1.
